meta.topic: Google ADK and Gemini Tool Calling
meta.title: Google ADK and Gemini Tool Calling
meta.thesis: Google ADK and Gemini Tool Calling is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A Gemini-based assistant schedules meetings and reads docs through approved tools. By the end, they should be able to build or review Google ADK tool-calling contract with schemas and review gates, measure valid tool calls with required arguments, and catch the failure where the model invents a tool argument that the backend never accepts.

modules.title: Gemini function calling returns structured action requests
modules.sub: The model selects a function and arguments; your code executes.
modules.summary: Function calling bridges natural language to application code.

blocks.title: The model proposes; the runtime disposes

spans.text: Problem anchor: a user asks “Schedule a project review with Maya tomorrow.” Gemini function calling can return a structured request such as `schedule_meeting(attendees, time)`, but the app must validate calendar access, time zone, conflicts, and approval.

Official Gemini docs frame function calling as connecting models to external tools and APIs. The model determines when to call a function and supplies parameters; client code performs the real action.
Never execute a function call before validating arguments and user authority.

blocks.analogy: Function calling is a filled-out work order, not the work itself.

spans.text: The model may return a meeting function with attendee and time fields. The app parses the call, validates required fields, checks policy, then either executes or asks the user to confirm.
If the model invents an attendee email or vague time, the app should request clarification rather than guessing.

items.text: Declare function name, description, and parameters.
Let Gemini propose a call when user intent matches.
Validate arguments and authority in application code.
Return tool result as context for final response.

modules.title: ADK LlmAgent packages model, instruction, and tools
modules.sub: An ADK agent gives tool calling a reusable product wrapper.
modules.summary: ADK turns a model-plus-tools pattern into an agent object.
objectives: Name LlmAgent fields such as model, instruction, description, and tools.

blocks.title: LlmAgent is the named tool-using worker

spans.text: Google ADK docs show `LlmAgent` configured with a model, name, description, instruction, and tools. Python can accept a native function directly as a tool, while other languages may use explicit FunctionTool wrappers or annotations.
The LLM uses tool names, descriptions, docstrings, and parameter schemas to decide which tool to call. That means tool naming and docstrings are behavioral design, not decoration.
A tool description should say when not to use the tool as clearly as when to use it.

blocks.analogy: An ADK LlmAgent is a job role plus a tool belt.

blocks.title: Case study: capital-city demo grows into product agent

spans.text: A simple agent answers capital-city questions with a function. In a product setting, the same pattern becomes a support agent with tools for KB search, ticket lookup, and draft reply creation.
The risk rises with tools: a search tool is low risk; a ticket update tool needs policy and approval.

items.text: Attach narrow tools with typed parameters.
Run sample prompts that should and should not call tools.
Inspect tool call arguments before execution.

modules.title: Session state and workflows add control
modules.sub: ADK can carry state and compose deterministic agent workflows.
modules.summary: ADK state and workflows are application control surfaces.

blocks.title: State is explicit context, not hidden intuition

spans.text: ADK session state can be injected into LlmAgent instructions with template keys such as `{topic}`. This is powerful for context-aware behavior, but values should be controlled product state, not random transcript leftovers.
ADK also documents workflow-style agents such as sequential, parallel, and loop patterns. Loop workflows need explicit termination mechanisms or max iterations.
For every state key used in instructions, name who writes it and when it expires.

blocks.analogy: Session state is a labeled control panel, not a junk drawer.

modules.title: Code a narrow FunctionTool-style agent
modules.sub: A small example should expose tool arguments and policy.
modules.summary: The useful example validates the call before the side effect.
objectives: Predict tool output and validation behavior.

blocks.title: Tool functions should stay small and typed

spans.text: For teaching, use a harmless function such as looking up a capital or checking availability. For product work, wrap side effects in policy and approval.
Spaced recall: from structured outputs, schemas help shape arguments but do not prove intent. Keep executor validation close to the function.
Add one malformed argument test before adding more tools.

blocks.title: Minimal ADK LlmAgent with a function tool
blocks.code:
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent

def get_capital_city(country: str) -> str:
    """Retrieves the capital city for a supported country."""
    capitals = {"france": "Paris", "japan": "Tokyo", "canada": "Ottawa"}
    return capitals.get(country.lower(), f"Unknown country: {country}")

capital_agent = LlmAgent(
    model="gemini-flash-latest",
    name="capital_agent",
    description="Answers capital-city questions for supported countries.",
    instruction="Use the tool for capital-city lookups. Do not invent unsupported capitals.",
    tools=[get_capital_city],
)

# In a real app, inspect the tool call and result in the ADK event stream.
print(get_capital_city("Japan"))
blocks.explanation: The function is harmless and typed. A real ADK run would let the agent request it, while the application inspects events and tool results.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before reading the answer, predict the printed output.
predictThenReveal.answer: It prints `Tokyo` because the function lowercases the country and finds `japan` in the dictionary.

modules.title: Evaluate tool calls, not just final replies
modules.sub: ADK/Gemini apps need traces, malformed-argument tests, and policy checks.
modules.summary: Tool-calling quality lives in the call trace.
objectives: Test tool selection and no-call cases.
Monitor session state and loop termination.

blocks.title: The tool trace is the evidence

spans.text: For Gemini function calling and ADK agents, evaluation should inspect whether the model chose the right tool, produced valid arguments, handled tool errors, respected session state, and avoided tools when it should answer directly.

For side effects, test approval gates and idempotency. For workflows, test loop termination and state updates. For integrations, date-stamp API assumptions because ADK versions and supported languages can evolve.
Include a prompt that looks like a tool request but lacks required details. The agent should ask for clarification.

blocks.title: Verify AI output from Google ADK/Gemini tool calling

spans.text: Review the event or tool trace with the final answer.

items.text: The selected function/tool matched the user intent and description.
Arguments passed schema and application policy before execution.
Session state used in instructions had a trusted writer and lifetime.
Side-effecting tools required approval or safe idempotency.
Loop or multi-agent workflows had explicit termination and eval cases.

blocks.title: Tool-call eval
blocks.prompt: What should a malformed scheduling request trigger?

options.text: A guessed time and automatic booking.
Clarification or validation failure before any calendar side effect.

blocks.explanation: The runtime should not execute vague or invalid tool calls.

questions.rot: Start with direct function calling for one step; move to ADK when session state, tools, agent delegation, or workflow control matter.
